title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Water
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: CISA lists the BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day as exploited; a suspected China-nexus espionage group has used it since late August
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-102764 in BeyondTrust Remote Support to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October; the 19 October federal deadline has passed. A day before the listing, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reported that a suspected China-nexus espionage group it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221) had exploited the flaw, rated CVSS v4.0 9.3 by its CNA, as a zero-day since late August. The intruders gained root on Remote Support appliances, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s file transfer to take documents. BeyondTrust shipped a fix on 8 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand. GTIG names no victims or sectors, no water utility has reported a compromise, and we found no new victim or attribution reporting since mid-October. It stays the lead because a confirmed intrusion campaign by a suspected state-linked group outranks this week’s PHP2Shell flaws, which are exploited and in KEV but have no confirmed victim organization; in our assessment, remote-support tools are also a common way integrators and SCADA vendors reach utility workstations. No attack on water control systems has been confirmed in the past 30 days.

items.title: Attackers took over internet-reachable refrigeration controllers at about 700 French supermarkets; France’s cyber agency says the campaign is probably still running
items.content_text: Over the nights of 11–13 October, attackers remotely changed settings on web-managed refrigeration controllers in French supermarkets, forcing long or continuous defrost cycles that delayed alarms and pushed some cases to around 50 °C. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 stores were hit, at chains including Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché/Netto and Monoprix; the Paris prosecutor has reported fires, and its cybercrime section has opened an inquiry. CERT-FR’s alert named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb units on 13 October, and says in its 16 October update that the campaigns are probably still ongoing; no new attack nights have been reported since 13 October, and the alert was still at that third version on 28 October. No group has claimed it, no ransom was demanded and the entry route has not been established; Danfoss says most affected units are end-of-life. Les Mousquetaires, which runs Intermarché and Netto, has said the intrusion came through a company that maintained refrigeration at some of its stores; that is the retailer’s statement, not an official finding. No water system is involved. In our assessment the method, remote setpoint changes on controllers left reachable from the internet, mirrors this year’s attacks on US water systems, and Nozomi’s 13 October analysis ties the same exposed-access weakness to them.

items.title: Symantec: a China-nexus Warlock ransomware crew breached a water utility through on-premises SharePoint
items.content_text: Symantec’s threat hunters reported on 1 October that a China-nexus threat actor it calls Longlegs (also tracked as Storm-2603) attacked at least four organizations in the past two months: a water utility, a telecom provider, a regional government body and a university, in Portuguese- and Spanish-speaking countries across Europe, Africa and Latin America. None is named. The group typically gets in by exploiting on-premises Microsoft SharePoint Server; the only CVEs Symantec names are the 2025 “ToolShell” flaws, plus related SharePoint bugs. It then uses a vulnerable signed driver to switch off security tools, a Visual Studio Code tunnel for persistence and the domain SYSVOL share to push ransomware. In Symantec’s detailed case study, an intrusion at an unnamed critical-infrastructure organization, Warlock reached at least 33 hosts; the report does not say whether that victim was the water utility, and it describes no OT or operational impact. In our assessment, a domain-wide ransomware push is exactly where a flat or over-trusted link between utility IT and SCADA turns an office outage into an operations problem.

items.title: FBI and Secret Service: the FortiBleed campaign against Fortinet firewalls is still active, and their warning covers the water sector
items.content_text: In a joint advisory dated 6 October, the FBI and US Secret Service said the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat. There is no CVE: the attackers log in with reused or leaked credentials, crack passwords stored with legacy SHA-256 hashing and sniff authentication traffic. Once in, they create their own administrator accounts and sometimes reset or delete the originals, locking owners out, and the access is resold; the advisory says brokers have passed it to INC/Lynx and Payload ransomware affiliates, and SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments. The advisory covers all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors and names water and wastewater among them; no water utility or control-system compromise has been described. SOCRadar’s count of 86,644 working device credentials in 194 countries dates from 19 June and is not a new figure. FortiGates often sit at a utility’s IT/OT boundary or carry vendor VPN access (editorial assessment).

items.title: Vicksburg, Mississippi ransomware takes city systems offline and disrupts utility bill payments
items.content_text: Vicksburg Mayor Willis Thompson said in a statement on 1 October that a ransomware attack forced the city to take systems offline temporarily, disrupting its utility payment systems; emergency services were not affected. He said no one’s service will be cut off and no late-payment penalties will be charged while the investigation runs, and that the city is still working out whether personal or confidential information was compromised. The FBI, DHS, state officials and private responders are helping. No group has claimed the attack, and the city has not commented on any ransom demand. The reporting does not say which utility services the billing covers, and nothing points to water or wastewater control systems being affected. It is an IT-side incident, but municipal utilities that share city IT, billing and accounts should know what a city-wide shutdown would take down with it (editorial assessment).

items.title: After France’s supermarket attacks, Forescout counts nearly 13,000 exposed refrigeration control services worldwide, and Waterfall sets out a minimum firewall checklist for small sites
items.content_text: Forescout’s Vedere Labs reported on 22 October that internet searches for ten refrigeration-controller product families returned 12,976 exposed service observations on 6,017 public IP addresses in 99 countries and territories; it counts services, not devices. About 80% of the Danfoss StoreView observations ran firmware older than 4.3.1, which carries known flaws, and Forescout counts more than 20 hacktivist claims of attacks on refrigeration systems since January, mostly in Spain and Italy (claims, not confirmed incidents). It says the entry route, actor and persistence in the French attacks are still unknown. Two days earlier, Waterfall Security’s Andrew Ginter, noting that the attacks look similar to recent ones on small US water utilities, set out a minimum setup for sites with little IT staff: a commercial-grade firewall with VPN, MFA and automatic updates; deny all traffic by default and allow only fixed addresses such as the service provider’s office, never home or mobile ones; back up and document the configuration; and replace the firewall about every four years. His theories about how the French attackers got in are his own and unconfirmed.
tags: Research — Internet exposure of remotely managed controllers after the French attacks; firewall guidance for small sites

items.title: MITRE ATT&CK v20 catalogues the July attacks on more than 30 Minnesota water utilities as campaign C0066
items.content_text: MITRE’s ATT&CK v20, released this month, adds campaign C0066, “2026 U.S. Water Utilities Attacks” (entry created 8 October, last modified 13 October). It covers intrusions from 27 July at more than 30 municipal water and wastewater utilities in Minnesota, part of wider activity the FBI and EPA reported in at least seven states. The attackers reached internet-facing Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs through cellular gateways at water towers and sewer lift stations and changed their IP addresses and passwords to lock operators out. At least one victim’s program logic was altered, and reported effects included loss of water pressure, flooding and one treatment plant taken offline. MITRE says the campaign has not been formally attributed. The release also adds CyberAv3ngers’ IOControl malware, a Mexican campaign (C0064) that reached a municipal water utility, and a new ICS scripting technique, T1701. C0066’s technique list, from default credentials to modified parameters and program logic, is a ready-made checklist for detection and tabletop work.

items.title: PHP2Shell: CISA lists both PHP flaws as exploited, Palo Alto reports attacks on exposed firewall management interfaces, and Schneider now has a fix for Control Engineering
items.content_text: CISA added both PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (each CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 26 October with a 29 October federal deadline. Researchers at Perplexity, with Expel’s Marcus Hutchins concurring, confirmed working remote code execution against a honeypot over 24–25 October; Sophos and Unit 42 withdrew earlier reports of successful attacks, CISA has not described the activity and no victim organization has been named. Palo Alto Networks raised its advisory to Critical on 27 October and says active exploitation has been observed against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet: the web interface and XML API on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and Panorama (GlobalProtect is not affected). Palo Alto rates it CVSS v4.0 9.2, or 5.2 when management access is restricted to trusted addresses, and is rolling out hotfixes through 30 October that, with one exception, also fix the Brotli decoder flaw CISA added to KEV on 27 October. Siemens says RUGGEDCOM APE1808 units running PAN-OS are affected, with remediation through Siemens support and Palo Alto’s workarounds. Schneider Electric’s notice SESB-2026-295-01, updated to version 2.0.0 on 26 October, now says remediation is available for EcoStruxure Control Engineering; Security Expert is fixed in 1.48.4.0. ABB says APROL up to R 4.4-65 is affected, with patches planned for 26 and 29 October, and Rockwell has confirmed no affected products while its review continues. PHP itself was fixed on 21 October in 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. In our assessment, the firewall between business IT and SCADA is now the most exposed point for utilities, followed by websites and payment portals that outside providers run on PHP.

items.title: Ivanti Connect Secure: a three-flaw chain gave attackers root on fully patched VPNs, and one link is still unpatched
items.content_text: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that attackers chained three flaws to run commands as root on fully patched Connect Secure VPN appliances at a limited number of customers. Two of the flaws are fixed under a single CVE, CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS v3.1 8.6), an authentication bypass that leads to unauthenticated command execution; the third, a privilege-escalation bug, had no CVE or patch at disclosure, and Ivanti promised a fix in the coming weeks; no Ivanti fix for it had been found as of 28 October. Volexity, which found the chain during an incident response, tracks the actor as a new group, UTA0576; Volexity and Defused date exploitation to at least early October (1–3 October). The intruders left no web shell; they stole domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, sprayed passwords and wiped logs. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 13 October with a 16 October deadline and warns that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker may not detect the compromise. No water-sector victim has been reported; Connect Secure is a common front door for utility staff and vendor remote access (editorial assessment).

items.title: Citrix NetScaler: a fourth critical flaw follows three exploited ones, and builds that fixed September’s zero-days need upgrading again
items.content_text: Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-107406 on 8 October (bulletin CTX697191), a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, rated CVSS v4.0 9.5. Citrix says it may allow code execution or denial of service and knows of no exploitation; it was still not in KEV as of CISA’s 27 October catalog. Builds that fixed the late-September zero-days stay exposed when used as a SAML identity provider, and CISA urged customers to patch on 9 October. The earlier trio is exploited and in KEV: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (added 27 September) and CVE-2026-88779 (added 4 October), which Citrix and watchTowr describe as a crash bug and which CISA says attackers use to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs. Google’s threat intelligence group counts dozens of affected organizations and Arctic Wolf at least 78 targeted; Shadowserver saw more than 20,000 exposed instances in late September. WaterISAC alerted members on 28 September, and no water-sector victim has been reported. NetScaler often fronts VPN and vendor access into utility networks (editorial assessment).

items.title: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: an exploited flaw that lets any logged-in user take operator control is now in CISA KEV
items.content_text: Arista disclosed CVE-2026-114625 on 22 October in Security Advisory 0199 and says it is known to be actively exploited. The SQL-injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the management console for VeloCloud SD-WAN, lets any authenticated user, down to the Enterprise Read Only role, impersonate a built-in superuser operator account and reach internal-only functions, putting the orchestrator and the data it manages at risk. Arista rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 / v4.0 9.4. Releases 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12 fix it; hosted and dedicated orchestrators have already been patched, and end-of-support versions were not assessed. Arista lists two attacker IP addresses but names no actor or victims. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, now passed. No water-sector victim has been reported. In our assessment, an SD-WAN orchestrator controls the links between a utility’s offices, treatment plants and remote sites, so a takeover reaches every site it manages.

items.title: Siemens Software Center: attackers abuse a DLL-loading flaw in a ClickFix malware campaign, and CISA adds it to KEV
items.content_text: Siemens confirmed on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, an uncontrolled search-path flaw in its Siemens Software Center Windows application, is being exploited. Attackers bundle a genuine, validly signed copy of the program with their own DLLs, so the trusted Siemens binary loads their code; Siemens ties the activity to the “Romulus” ClickFix campaign, which lures users into running the files themselves, and says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached to its knowledge. It names no final malware. Siemens rates the flaw CVSS v3.1 6.7 / v4.0 8.4 and fixed it in V4.0.9.8; existing installations update automatically on next start. CISA added it to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November federal deadline and republished the advisory as ICSA-26-295-03 on 22 October. In our assessment, the risk for utilities sits on engineering and SCADA workstations: application-allowlisting rules that trust anything Siemens-signed would let such a bundle run.

items.title: A FortiManager breach at a managed service provider exposed settings for 500-plus client firewalls; the FortiOS flaw used to gain root is now in KEV
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October that attackers broke into a telecommunications managed service provider through its FortiManager, using the 2024 “FortiJump” flaw CVE-2024-47575, then used CVE-2025-61624, a FortiOS command-line path-traversal flaw, to get root on managed FortiGate firewalls and plant a loader Unit 42 calls PEERSTITCH. The stolen archive held configuration data for more than 500 FortiGates protecting the provider and its clients; Unit 42 calls that exposure of configuration and credential material, not confirmed intrusion into the client networks. It tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954 (also UNC5820) and names no state. Fortinet fixed CVE-2025-61624 in April, rates it Medium and says it needs privileged, authenticated access; CISA added it to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October deadline. The CVE record lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, which can run FortiOS, among affected products. Many small utilities have their firewalls managed by an outside provider (editorial assessment).

items.title: MikroTik RouterOS: three flaws now in CISA KEV, and a new pre-authentication CVSS 9.8 bug in a 29 September CISA advisory
items.content_text: CISA’s exploited list now holds three RouterOS flaws: CVE-2026-86060 and CVE-2026-67277, added 10 September, and CVE-2026-67279, an authentication bypass added 25 September with a 28 September federal deadline. Chained with CVE-2026-86060, CVE-2026-67279 lets an attacker take administrative control of an internet-exposed router without a password; CERT Polska corrected the chain on 22 September, so earlier reports that named other CVE IDs in it were wrong. Fixes came on 3 September in RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21, and exploitation is reported from as early as 2 September. Separately, CISA advisory ICSA-26-272-06 (29 September, updated 30 September) covers CVE-2026-84411, an integer underflow in HTTP request handling that is reachable before login and could allow remote code execution or a crash, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8. CISA lists every RouterOS version below 7.24 as affected and reports no known exploitation; it is not in KEV. MikroTik routers are widely used at small utilities’ remote sites and as cellular or VPN gateways (editorial assessment).

items.title: FortiMail and Cisco SD-WAN Manager zero-days join CISA’s exploited list; Fortinet now lists fixed releases
items.content_text: Two more internet-facing products were confirmed exploited at the turn of the month. Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-175, published 1 October, covers CVE-2026-104286 (CVSS 9.8), a path-traversal flaw in the web interface of FortiMail’s identity-based encryption feature that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the system. Fortinet says it has been reported exploited in the wild, and CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2; the 7.2 branch must move to 7.4 or later. Cisco disclosed on 30 September that CVE-2026-76504 (CVSS 9.8) in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager lets a remote attacker bypass an authentication rule on an API endpoint and gain administrator access; Cisco says it saw active exploitation in September, CISA listed it the same day with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised its advisory on 2 October. Neither vendor has named an actor or victims. In our assessment, FortiMail sits in the corporate mail path that utility staff and vendors rely on, and an SD-WAN manager can control the links to treatment plants and remote pumping sites.
tags: Advisory — Two more exploited edge zero-days in CISA KEV: FortiMail and Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager

items.title: CISA republishes Mitsubishi Electric’s ICONICS advisory: fixes for GENESIS64 and GENESIS, none for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz
items.content_text: CISA republished Mitsubishi Electric advisory 2026-006 as ICSA-26-300-02 on 27 October, twelve days after the vendor released it. It covers flaws across Mitsubishi’s ICONICS SCADA, HMI and historian products. The highest-rated, CVE-2026-16438 (CVSS v3.1 9.1 in Mitsubishi’s advisory), gives the administrator account default DCOM permissions. CVE-2026-16436 (v3.1 8.1) is a shared, fixed challenge-response that can unlock any user account once an attacker obtains the response; the advisory also lists a second challenge-response flaw, CVE-2026-16437 (v3.1 6.4), and the older libwebp bug CVE-2023-4863 (v3.1 8.2). Affected are GENESIS up to 11.03 and GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX up to 10.97.3; version 10.98 and GENESIS 11.04 fix them (10.97.3 for libwebp). MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz, all versions, will get no fix, and Mitsubishi advises replacing them with GENESIS64 or GENESIS. No exploitation is reported and none of the flaws is in KEV. CISA’s republication lists only Critical Manufacturing as the sector, but GENESIS64 also runs SCADA and HMI screens in water and wastewater (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA flags WAGO controller and Moxa edge-gateway flaws, both listing water and wastewater: a low-privilege command injection to root and a hard-coded key
items.content_text: CISA’s 20 October batch includes two advisories that name Water and Wastewater Systems among the affected sectors. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes CERT@VDE’s VDE-2026-096 for WAGO CC100, PFC100 G2, PFC200 G2, TP600, Edge Controller and WP400 devices on firmware older than 4.10.0 (FW32). CVE-2026-80466 (CVSS v3.1 8.8) lets a logged-in, low-privileged user inject operating-system commands through routing settings in the web-based management interface, which a root helper then runs; CVE-2026-88850 (v3.1 8.1) lets low-privileged users change root-owned PROFIBUS settings. Firmware 4.10.0 (FW32) fixes both. ICSA-26-293-03 covers Moxa AIG-302 ThingsPro Edge gateways up to firmware 1.4.0: CVE-2026-109813, a hard-coded cryptographic key (v3.1 8.1 / v4.0 8.6), and a missing-authorization flaw, CVE-2026-109812 (v3.1 6.8 / v4.0 6.9); version 1.4.1 fixes both. Neither advisory reports exploitation, and neither is in KEV. Controllers and gateways like these often sit in pump-station and telemetry panels (editorial assessment).
tags: Advisory — CISA ICS advisories for controller and edge-gateway firmware; Water and Wastewater listed; no known exploitation

items.title: October OT patches: Siemens S7-1500 web-server flaws have no fix yet; Schneider Sage RTUs and Ignition get updates
items.content_text: Siemens’ 13 October release includes SSA-591731, eight web-server flaws in S7-1500, ET 200SP, ET 200pro and Drive Controller CPUs, rated up to CVSS v3.1 9.6 (v4.0 9.4), that could let an attacker run code in a logged-in user’s browser and carry out PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations are available so far. A separate advisory, SSA-784472, lists 377 flaws in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP module, also without a fix. Schneider Electric’s SEVD-2026-286-02 covers Sage RTUs (1410, 1430, 1450, 2400, 3030 Magnum and 4400) that do not properly verify firmware, so a modified image could be loaded when an administrator runs an update (CVE-2026-102250, CVSS v3.1 7.2 / v4.0 8.6); firmware C3414-500-S02L0 fixes it. CISA also flagged an Ignition SCADA privilege-escalation flaw, CVE-2026-92817 (CVSS v3.1 8.8), fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9. CISA republished Siemens’ 13 October advisories on 22 October (ICSA-26-295-02 to -18), and the S7 web-server and TM MFP issues still had no fix. None is known to be exploited or listed in KEV. S7-1500 PLCs, Sage RTUs and Ignition all turn up in water and wastewater SCADA (editorial assessment).

items.title: WaterISAC: Fortinet has shipped fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, with flaw details held until 10 November
items.content_text: WaterISAC told members in a TLP:CLEAR notification on 27 October that Fortinet has released coordinated security fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, and that CVE IDs, CVSS scores and technical details are due in Fortinet’s PSIRT advisories on 10 November. WaterISAC says no active exploitation has been reported so far, but warns that attackers can study the fixes to build exploits before then, and that vulnerability scanners will not flag affected devices until CVE data exists, so versions must be checked directly. The fixed releases it lists are FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9 (7.2 users should move to 7.4 or later); and FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. FortiSASE has been updated automatically, and FortiManager Cloud may need a manual update. These details come from WaterISAC; we have not seen a public Fortinet notice. FortiGate firewalls often sit at a utility’s IT/OT boundary or carry vendor VPN access (editorial assessment).

items.title: Moxa: its remote-access client can be fooled by a fake server, and an end-of-life OnCell cellular gateway has flaws that will not be fixed
items.content_text: Moxa advisory MPSA-269510, published 27 October, covers three flaws. In the Moxa Remote Connect (MRC) Client, an OpenVPN-based remote-access tool, CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6, scored by Moxa) means the client accepts a configuration from the server without properly validating the server’s certificate, so an attacker on the network path could pose as the MRC server; versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0 are affected, and 4.2.2, available through Moxa support, fixes it. The OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway ships static HTTPS and CA private keys in its firmware (CVE-2026-111460, v4.0 7.7) and has a command-injection flaw in its SMS upgrade feature, reachable by a privileged attacker when SMS management is enabled (CVE-2026-111461, v4.0 7.5). The gateway is end-of-life, so neither will be fixed; the mitigations are to reset the device so it generates new keys and to keep SMS management disabled, as it is by default. No exploitation has been reported and none of the three is in KEV. Cellular gateways connect lift stations, tanks and wells to SCADA, and integrators use remote-connect clients to reach them (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA flags open-source code inside OT products: an lwIP SMTP-client overflow rated 9.8 and six Eclipse Milo OPC UA flaws
items.content_text: Two CISA advisories this month name Water and Wastewater Systems among the affected sectors for flaws in widely reused open-source code. ICSA-26-279-02 (6 October) covers CVE-2026-15340, a buffer overflow in the SMTP client of the lwIP embedded TCP/IP stack, version 2.2.1, rated CVSS v3.1 9.8; it is fixed by an upstream patch rather than a new release, and real-world exposure depends on whether a device maker uses lwIP’s SMTP client at all. ICSA-26-288-01 (15 October) covers six flaws in Eclipse Milo, a Java OPC UA client and server library, the highest rated CVSS v3.1 8.2; version 1.1.5 fixes them, and the older 0.6.x line will get no fix. Neither is in KEV, and no exploitation has been reported. The practical exposure sits in the products that embed these components, which makes this a question for your SCADA, telemetry and instrument vendors (editorial assessment).

items.title: Lantronix G520 cellular gateway flaws could let an attacker swap firmware and run code as root
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-272-01, released 29 September, covers two flaws in Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateways running firmware 2.6.0.4R6_stable: CVE-2026-91191, improper verification of a cryptographic signature, and CVE-2026-84409, a cross-site scripting bug, each rated CVSS v3.1 7.5 (v4 7.7). CISA says exploitation could let an attacker replace the device software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. It lists Water and Wastewater Systems among the affected sectors, alongside Energy and Transportation Systems, and says the product is deployed worldwide. Firmware 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both, and no known public exploitation has been reported to CISA. Cellular gateways like this often connect lift stations, tanks and other unstaffed sites to SCADA, so a compromised unit sits directly on the control path (editorial assessment).

items.title: CISA’s new four-year strategy, “CISA 2030”, names operational technology security as a priority and starts a review of the agency’s core services
items.content_text: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October. Its three pillars cover day-to-day defense, longer-term hardening and resilience to disruption, and the plan commits the agency to put its resources where they will have the greatest impact, including assessing which infrastructure matters most through a national risk register and studying how assets depend on one another. Under the Defend pillar CISA says it will help operators improve OT security, with asset visibility and intrusion detection named, and it gives supply-chain security particular attention. The agency will begin reviewing its core services and capabilities within 60 days, finish an implementation plan with success metrics within 180 days and report on progress after a year. Acting Director Nick Andersen describes a shift to a more “anticipatory” stance. The strategy creates no new requirements for utilities, and water and wastewater are not singled out in the coverage we reviewed. Utilities that use CISA’s free assessments, scanning or regional advisors should watch the outcome of the services review (editorial assessment).

items.title: EPA will run a free webinar on 18 November on designing tabletop exercises for drinking water and wastewater utilities
items.content_text: WaterISAC posted on 22 October that EPA will host a free one-hour webinar on 18 November, 1–2 p.m. ET, on building a tabletop exercise with EPA’s TTX Tool for drinking water and wastewater utilities (ttx.epa.gov). EPA will explain why tabletop exercises are worth the time, an exercise designer who has used the tool will share lessons, and a utility that recently took part in one will describe the experience; attendees are invited to bring questions. WaterISAC’s post does not include a registration link, so watch EPA’s water-security pages and WaterISAC channels for sign-up details. In our assessment, MITRE’s C0066 entry for this summer’s attacks on Minnesota water utilities gives a ready-made scenario for a first exercise.

items.title: Accenture, Dragos and SANS launch a foundation offering free OT monitoring, deployment and training to up to 500 small utilities, water and wastewater included
items.content_text: Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute announced the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation on 20 October: a nonprofit with about $10 million in initial funding and services, with technology support from Elastic. Its first phase covers up to 500 utilities with annual revenue under $100 million, a threshold the companies say covers 97% of utilities, on top of the more than 100 already in Dragos’s Community Defense Program. The foundation’s site lists water, wastewater, electric and natural-gas utilities in the US and Canada; Dragos’s announcement refers to US utilities. Members get the Dragos Platform, Neighborhood Keeper and OT-CERT; assessment, deployment and ongoing support from Accenture; SANS training with GIAC certification; and hardware funding where needed. Enrollment “opens soon” and an interest list is open now. There is no government involvement. In our assessment, this removes the cost barrier for small systems that have never had OT network monitoring; finding staff time to act on it is the harder part.

items.title: CISA’s final cyber incident-reporting rule reaches White House review; text and start dates are not yet public
items.content_text: The White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs logged receipt of CISA’s final rule under the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (RIN 1670-AA04) on 1 October, and the review is pending. The statute set an October 2025 deadline, and CISA’s later targets of May and September 2026 slipped; HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before year-end. The law calls for covered entities to report covered cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours, but no obligation applies until the final rule sets its dates. The rule text, including which water and wastewater systems it covers, is not public, and the review can still change it. No publication of the final rule had been reported as of 28 October.
